title: Resolution urging airline service contractors operating at San Francisco International Airport to protect workers and to create and maintain as many full-time jobs as the flight schedules will allow.
raw_text:
FILE NO. 220713 RESOLUTION NO. 288-72
1 [Urging Airline Service Contractors to Maintain Full Time Work for Employees]
2
3 Resolution urging airline service contractors operating at San Francisco International
4 Airport to protect workers and to create and maintain as many full-time jobs as the
5 flight schedules will allow.
6
7 WHEREAS, The San Francisco Board of Supervisors acted during the COVID-19
8 pandemic to ensure that low wage, immigrant, and essential workers of color were protected,
9 passing critical pieces of legislation, including the Healthy Airport Ordinance, to ensure that
10 airport workers had access to fully paid family healthcare; and
11 WHEREAS, Airport workers faced months of unemployment and dangerous working
12 conditions during the pandemic; and
13 WHEREAS, The San Francisco Board of Supervisors has worked to ensure that these
14 most impacted communities are prioritized in the economic recovery; and
15 WHEREAS, With a contracted airline service workforce made up largely of Black,
16 Brown and immigrant service workers, this industry's recovery presents both racial justice and
17 economic justice concerns; and
18 WHEREAS, The domestic recovery of the airline is well underway with national travel
19 activity already in excess of 90% of pre-pandemic levels; and
20 WHEREAS, Airline contractors received billions in CARES Act bailout money in
21 addition to over $50 billion given to their client airlines, and the airline industry prior to COVID
22 was coming off of its most successful decades ever and five of the most profitable years in
23 industry history; and
24
25
Supervisors Mandelman; Walton, Mar. Preston, Chan, Ronen, Safai
BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Page 1
1 WHEREAS, Contracted out passenger service workers at SFO report that despite
2 increased business at the airport, many are working part-time schedules while experiencing
3 increased workload and unsafe staffing levels; and
4 WHEREAS, Airline employers cutting worker's hours undermines San Francisco's
5 living wage laws and airport safety standards, pushing experienced workers out of the
6 industry; now, therefore, be it
7 RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors of the City and County of San Francisco
8 hereby urges airline service contractors operating at San Francisco International Airport and
9 their airline clients to create and maintain as many full-time jobs as the flight schedule will
10 allow; and, be it
11 FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors hereby urges the airline service
12 contractors to settle a fair union contract with SEIU USWW that protects full-time work and
13 provides for good family sustaining jobs.

title: Resolution urging Governor Gavin Newsom and the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control to delay implementation of the Responsible Beverage Service Training Program.
raw_text:
FILE NO. 220712 RESOLUTION NO. 287-22
1 [Urging to Delay Implementation of the Responsible Beverage Service Training Program]
2
3 Resolution urging Governor Gavin Newsom and the Department of Alcoholic Beverage
4 Control to delay implementation of the Responsible Beverage Service Training
5 Program.
6
7 WHEREAS, California State Assembly Bill No. 1221 (AB 1221) established the
8 Responsible Beverage Service (RBS) Training Program Act of 2017, and required the
9 Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control (ABC) to develop, implement, and administer a
10 curriculum for an RBS training program; and
11 WHEREAS, The RBS requires alcohol servers to complete a training course offered or
12 authorized by ABC focused on laws governing alcoholic beverages and the impact of alcohol
13 on the body in order to promote safer consumption of alcoholic drinks; and
14 WHEREAS, Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, the RBS training requirement was
15 delayed for a year to July 1 , 2022, with mandatory training to be completed by August 31,
16 2022;and
17 WHEREAS, San Francisco businesses were provided this information in May 2022,
18 with information only available in English and Spanish; and
19 WHEREAS, While other languages including Chinese, Filipino, and Vietnamese will be
20 available for businesses by July 1, 2022, the delay to offer additional languages shortens the
21 window in which small, immigrant-owned businesses can come into compliance; and
22 WHEREAS, As of May 9, 2022, approximately 22,000 alcohol servers have been
23 successfully certified out of an estimated one million servers in California; and
24
25
Supervisors Chan; Peskin, Mar, Walton
BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Page 1
1 WHEREAS, ABC has approved only 35 trainers to educate the remaining hundreds of
2 thousands of servers, with an overwhelming majority in English and only a few in Spanish;
3 and
4 WHEREAS, Requiring businesses to be in compliance with this new program by
5 August 31, 2022 is not nearly enough time to conduct outreach and education to non-native
6 and limited English proficient speakers; and
7 WHEREAS, Servers who are not in compliance with the training requirements could
8 subject businesses to disciplinary action, including revocation of their liquor license; and
9 WHEREAS, While ABC has stated that the department will take an education-first
10 approach to enforcement, they have not provided a timeline for when enforcement measures
11 will be enacted, disproportionately impacting non-native and limited English-speaking servers
12 and immigrant-owned small businesses; and
13 WHEREAS, Immigrant-owned small businesses that disproportionately struggled
14 through the pandemic, facing racism and prejudice, are now being faced with a tight timeline
15 to come into compliance with the RBS, which represents an additional barrier to recovery;
16 now, therefore, be it
17 RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors of the City and County of San Francisco
18 urges Governor Gavin Newsom and the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control to delay
19 implementation of the Responsible Beverage Service Training Program; and, be it
20 FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors of the City and County of San
21 Francisco urges Governor Newsom and the Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control to
22 create a robust outreach plan to non-native and limited English proficient servers and
23 businesses, and expedite hiring of non-English speaking trainers; and, be it

title: Resolution urging St. Mary's Medical Center and Dignity Health to return to the bargaining table in order to negotiate contract language that protects the rights of resident physicians and attracts medical students to San Francisco to complete their residency.
raw_text:

1 [Urging St. Mary's Medical Center and Dignity Health to Negotiate in Good Faith]
2
3 Resolution urging St. Mary's Medical Center and Dignity Health to return to the
4 bargaining table in order to negotiate contract language that protects the rights of
5 resident physicians and attracts medical students to San Francisco to complete their
6 residency.
7
8 WHEREAS, The Committee of Interns and Residents - Service Employees
9 International Union (CIR-SEIU) represents resident physicians at St. Mary's Medical Center,
10 which is an affiliate of Dignity Health, and are currently engaged in contract negotiations; and
11 WHEREAS, Resident Physicians within CIR-SEIU have been on the frontlines of the
12 COVID-19 pandemic and are the primary caregivers for the sick, the vulnerable, the acute and
13 other disenfranchised constituents across the City and County of San Francisco; and
14 WHEREAS, St. Mary's Medical Center's resident physicians are experiencing high
15 rates of stress and burnout that are only exacerbated by financial anxiety caused by the high
16 cost of housing in San Francisco, accelerated inflation, and increasing student debt, which
17 averages a quarter million dollars per resident physician; and
18 WHEREAS, The physician shortage in California and San Francisco is worsening and
19 there are estimates of a statewide shortfall of 4,700 primary care providers and an additional
20 4,100 providers by the year 2030; and
21 WHEREAS, In the most recent academic year, St. Mary's Medical Center was unable
22 to attract a full complement of medical students who ranked this program among their
23 possible residency options, suggesting a lack of competitive pay and benefits; and
24 WHEREAS, Data shows that a physician is 55% more likely to stay in a community
25 where they conduct their residency; and
Supeivisors Chan; Preston, Walton. Safai
BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Page 1
1 WHEREAS, San Francisco has become the most expensive place to live in the state of
2 California, and one of the most expensive in the United States; and
3 WHEREAS, St. Mary's Medical Center is the lowest paid residency program in San
4 Francisco and the East Bay; and
5 WHEREAS, Collective bargaining is the most effective way for resident physicians at
6 St. Mary's Medical Center to secure safe working conditions and salaries and benefits that
7 allow them to live and work in San Francisco and continue to provide high quality patient care;
8 and
9 WHEREAS, A labor dispute involving Resident Physicians at St. Mary's and their
10 employer will likely result in the disruption of necessary patient care and life saving medical
11 treatments for San Francisco residents; and
12 WHEREAS, A strong collective bargaining agreement can be a tool to attract the best
13 and brightest medical students from across the country to complete their residency in San

1 [Supporting Funding for San Francisco Unified School District Early College Programs]
2
3 Resolution supporting funding for the Early College 2022 summer internship program
4 through allowed uses for education-designated funds and expansion of Dual
5 Enrollment for San Francisco Unified School District high school students through
6 prior year allocations.
7
8 WHEREAS, The San Francisco Unified School District (SFUSD) broadens
9 opportunities for high school students through on-ramps to post-secondary success through
10 an array of programs including: Career and Technical Education Pathways and Academies
11 tailored to SFUSD high schools, Work-Based Learning in partnership with businesses and
12 organizations, College Preparation Courses, and Early College; and
13 WHEREAS, The SFUSD College & Career Readiness team delivers programs that
14 provide students from under resourced communities with points of entry and opportunities to
15 explore interests in a real-world setting, and its Early College program has ensured access for
16 SFUSD equity and BIPOC groups while conducting broad outreach to high schools; this
17 programming involves close coordination with both SFUSD and City College of San Francisco
18 administration and personnel in the successful implementation of its Early College summer
19 program, as well as academic year Dual Enrollment for eligible high school students; and
20 WHEREAS, Early College offers a unique summer opportunity for SFUSD high school
21 students to engage in paid internships, learning experiences on the job, and options to take
22 City College credit courses supporting their career explorations in areas like child
23 development, health care, and business, and demand for this popular program has exceeded
24 capacity with over 1900 applicants this year; and
25
Supervisors Mar; Ronen, Preston, Mandelman
BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Page 1
1 WHEREAS, The Early College summer program complements other City initiatives
2 including Opportunities for All serving 13-24 year-olds, Mayor's Youth Employment &
3 Education Program lowering workforce barriers for high school students, YouthWorks
4 providing public sector internships for junior and senior high school students in San Francisco;
5 and
6 WHEREAS, Funding for the Early College summer program from funding through
7 excess Education Revenue Augmentation Fund sources were depleted in 2021, as a
8 fluctuating source from property tax collections that is not designed for funding ongoing
9 programs, and the Board of Supervisors recognized the value of Early College internships
10 along with other community serving programs and passed a budget supplemental (File
11 #210177) signed by Mayor Breed on April 9, 2021; this appropriation included $2.7 million to
12 Early College for the summer 2021 program, tasking SF Department of Children, Youth and
13 Their Families with administering the fund allocation to SFUSD; and
14 WHEREAS, The summer 2021 program served over 800 SFUSD students across 18
15 high schools with internship placements, with nearly 500 also completing a college course
16 connected to their internship, and the interns reflected the racial/ethnic diversity of SFUSD,
17 including hiring three times more African American, Latinx, and Pacific Islander students than
18 in previous years; and
19 WHEREAS, The Early College model builds in the student support needed for students
20 who face socioeconomic and other barriers to attending college, such as counselor outreach,
21 textbooks and digital access, internship supervision and placement coordination; and
22 WHEREAS, Dual Enrollment offers high school students at SFUSD and other
23 institutions the opportunity to take college courses offered by City College of San Francisco,

Resolution supporting funding for the Early College 2022 summer internship program
through allowed uses for education-designated funds and expansion of Dual
Enrollment for San Francisco Unified School District high school students through
prior year allocations.
WHEREAS, The San Francisco Unified School District (SFUSD) broadens
opportunities for high school students through on-ramps to post-secondary success through
an array of programs including: Career and Technical Education Pathways and Academies
tailored to SFUSD high schools, Work-Based Learning in partnership with businesses and
organizations, College Preparation Courses, and Early College; and
WHEREAS, The SFUSD College & Career Readiness team delivers programs that
provide students from under resourced communities with points of entry and opportunities to
explore interests in a real-world setting, and its Early College program has ensured access for
SFUSD equity and BIPOC groups while conducting broad outreach to high schools; this
programming involves close coordination with both SFUSD and City College of San Francisco
administration and personnel in the successful implementation of its Early College summer
program, as well as academic year Dual Enrollment for eligible high school students; and
WHEREAS, Early College offers a unique summer opportunity for SFUSD high school
students to engage in paid internships, learning experiences on the job, and options to take
City College credit courses supporting their career explorations in areas like child
development, health care, and business, and demand for this popular program has exceeded
capacity with over 1900 applicants this year; and
WHEREAS, The Early College summer program complements other City initiatives
including Opportunities for All serving 13-24 year-olds, Mayor's Youth Employment &
Education Program lowering workforce barriers for high school students, YouthWorks
providing public sector internships for junior and senior high school students in San Francisco;
and
WHEREAS, Funding for the Early College summer program from funding through
excess Education Revenue Augmentation Fund sources were depleted in 2021, as a
fluctuating source from property tax collections that is not designed for funding ongoing
programs, and the Board of Supervisors recognized the value of Early College internships
along with other community serving programs and passed a budget supplemental (File
#210177) signed by Mayor Breed on ; this appropriation included $2.7 million to
Early College for the summer 2021 program, tasking SF Department of Children, Youth and
Their Families with administering the fund allocation to SFUSD; and
WHEREAS, The summer 2021 program served over 800 SFUSD students across 18
high schools with internship placements, with nearly 500 also completing a college course
connected to their internship, and the interns reflected the racial/ethnic diversity of SFUSD,
including hiring three times more African American, Latinx, and Pacific Islander students than
in previous years; and
WHEREAS, The Early College model builds in the student support needed for students
who face socioeconomic and other barriers to attending college, such as counselor outreach,
textbooks and digital access, internship supervision and placement coordination; and
WHEREAS, Dual Enrollment offers high school students at SFUSD and other
institutions the opportunity to take college courses offered by City College of San Francisco,
providing on-ramps for higher education with exposure to potential majors and career
pathways, options to engage in curricula not taught at SFUSD, while offering degree-
applicable college units along with the option of SFUSD credits applied to high school
completion; and
WHEREAS, The current class allocations for Dual Enrollment do not meet all the
requests from SFUSD high schools, and these classes are in demand as many are taught on
the SFUSD campus, through California State Assembly Bill No. 288 provisions making it
convenient for high school students to enroll; in addition, these classes provide an alternative
to Advanced Placement (AP) courses for earning college credit while in high school, in
subjects like psychology, administration of justice, Spanish and Chinese, that appeal to more
diverse populations, with class offerings selected to meet graduation requirements at public
universities; now, therefore, be it
RESOLVED, That the City support Early College summer 2022 with funding to deliver
a robust program from eligible sources to cover summer internships, classes and student
support, among those, amounts identified as excess reserves in the Free City funds that are
stipulated to be returned to the General Fund when the reserve cap is exceeded, and other
sources deemed appropriate for funding pre-college initiatives for SFUSD high school
students; and, be it
FURTHER RESOLVED, That $1 million already identified in 2021 for supporting City
College courses be allocated for expansion of these courses in the Dual Enrollment
framework for SFUSD students in the 2022-23 academic year; and, be it
FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors join the Mayor's office in
supporting these vital programs for the City's youth to provide real world opportunities, access
to higher education, and connection to academic, material and social emotional supports for
their transition to adulthood.

title: Resolution urging the Department of Public Health, in consultation with the Department of Emergency Management, Mayor’s Office of Violence Prevention and Public Safety, Fire Department, Police Department, Department of Children, Youth, and Their Families, Department on the Status of Women, other relevant City departments, and community partners to create and adopt a publicly-available protocol to respond proactively to instances of gun-related community trauma.

AMENDED IN BOARD
FILE NO. 220615 5/24/2022 RESOLUTION NO. 255-22
1 [Urging the Development of Proactive Citywide Trauma Response to Gun Violence]
2
3 Resolution urging the Department of Public Health, in consultation with the Department
4 of Emergency Management, Mayor's Office of Violence Prevention and Public Safety,
5 Fire Department, Police Department, Department of Youth, and Families, Department
6 on the Status of Women, other relevant City departments, and community partners to
7 create and adopt a publicly-available protocol to respond proactively to instances of
8 gun-related community trauma.
9
10 WHEREAS, San Francisco continues to experience gun violence in our communities;
11 and
12 WHEREAS, Gun violence disproportionately impacts low-income Black and brown
13 communities; and
14 WHEREAS, Gun violence has deeply traumatic effects on direct victims, witnesses,
15 and nearby community members in serious and lasting ways; and
16 WHEREAS, Communities are strongest when they have resilience, self-determination,
17 and resources; and
18 WHEREAS, Community trauma can erode a community's capacity to thrive, address
19 issues, and exercise its collective efficacy; and
20 WHEREAS, According to the Center for Disease Control (CDC), community violence
21 has wide-reaching effects and can cause significant physical injuries and mental health
22 conditions such as depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder; and
23 WHEREAS, According to the CDC, communities experiencing violence may lead to
24 increased risk of developing chronic diseases because concerns about violence may prevent
25 them from walking, bicycling, and using parks or other recreational spaces; and
Supervisor Preston; Walton, Ronen, Chan, Mar, Safai
BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Page 1
1 WHEREAS, Communities deserve to feel safe and, when an incident occurs that
2 erodes their sense of safety, deserve to be supported; and
3 WHEREAS, Mental health resources can be instrumental in healing communities that
4 experience gun violence; and
5 WHEREAS, San Francisco has practices and partnerships in place to ensure that
6 direct victims of gun violence and their immediate families can get support, services,
7 counseling, and other resources to aid in their recovery; and
8 WHEREAS, San Francisco has trauma response resources available through its
9 Comprehensive Crisis Services team and through community-based organizations serving
10 high-risk communities; and
11 WHEREAS, No protocol currently exists to ensure that the City reaches out to affected
12 community members other than immediate victim(s) or their family members to connect them
13 to available trauma counseling resources in a timely manner; and
14 WHEREAS, Community members experiencing trauma after gun violence in their
15 neighborhoods should not have to go out of their way to receive information about available
16 resources or trauma counseling services; and
17 WHEREAS, A proactive trauma response would help remove existing barriers and
18 ensure that communities that have experienced gun violence can be connected to trauma
19 counseling resources they need; and
20 WHEREAS, Studies show that trauma counseling, in connection with other community
21 resources, can help prevent further violence; and
22 WHEREAS, Our city has protocols in place for community support after traumatic
23 events in other contexts, such as the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency's
24 response after fatal traffic collisions and the San Francisco Police Department's town halls
25
Supervisor Preston; Walton, Ronen, Chan, Mar, Safai
BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Page 2
1 after police shootings, which may offer guidance regarding coordination, outreach, and
2 response after incidents of gun violence; now, therefore, be it
3 RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors urges the Department of Public Health, in
4 consultation with the Department of Emergency Management, Mayor's Office of Violence
5 Prevention and Public Safety, San Francisco Fire Department, San Francisco Police
6 Department, Department of Youth, and Families, Department on the Status of Women, other
7 relevant City departments, and community partners to create a proposed protocol and

Resolution urging the Department of Public Health, in consultation with the Department
of Emergency Management, Mayor's Office of Violence Prevention and Public Safety,
Fire Department, Police Department, Department of Youth, and Families, Department
on the Status of Women, other relevant City departments, and community partners to
create and adopt a publicly-available protocol to respond proactively to instances of
gun-related community trauma.
WHEREAS, San Francisco continues to experience gun violence in our communities;
and
WHEREAS, Gun violence disproportionately impacts low-income Black and brown
communities; and
WHEREAS, Gun violence has deeply traumatic effects on direct victims, witnesses,
and nearby community members in serious and lasting ways; and
WHEREAS, Communities are strongest when they have resilience, self-determination,
and resources; and
WHEREAS, Community trauma can erode a community's capacity to thrive, address
issues, and exercise its collective efficacy; and
WHEREAS, According to the Center for Disease Control (CDC), community violence
has wide-reaching effects and can cause significant physical injuries and mental health
conditions such as depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder; and
WHEREAS, According to the CDC, communities experiencing violence may lead to
increased risk of developing chronic diseases because concerns about violence may prevent
them from walking, bicycling, and using parks or other recreational spaces; and
WHEREAS, Communities deserve to feel safe and, when an incident occurs that
erodes their sense of safety, deserve to be supported; and
WHEREAS, Mental health resources can be instrumental in healing communities that
experience gun violence; and
WHEREAS, San Francisco has practices and partnerships in place to ensure that
direct victims of gun violence and their immediate families can get support, services,
counseling, and other resources to aid in their recovery; and
WHEREAS, San Francisco has trauma response resources available through its
Comprehensive Crisis Services team and through community-based organizations serving
high-risk communities; and
WHEREAS, No protocol currently exists to ensure that the City reaches out to affected
community members other than immediate victim(s) or their family members to connect them
to available trauma counseling resources in a timely manner; and
WHEREAS, Community members experiencing trauma after gun violence in their
neighborhoods should not have to go out of their way to receive information about available
resources or trauma counseling services; and
WHEREAS, A proactive trauma response would help remove existing barriers and
ensure that communities that have experienced gun violence can be connected to trauma
counseling resources they need; and
WHEREAS, Studies show that trauma counseling, in connection with other community
resources, can help prevent further violence; and
WHEREAS, Our city has protocols in place for community support after traumatic
events in other contexts, such as the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency's
response after fatal traffic collisions and the San Francisco Police Department's town halls
after police shootings, which may offer guidance regarding coordination, outreach, and
response after incidents of gun violence; now, therefore, be it
RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors urges the Department of Public Health, in
consultation with the Department of Emergency Management, Mayor's Office of Violence
Prevention and Public Safety, San Francisco Fire Department, San Francisco Police
Department, Department of Youth, and Families, Department on the Status of Women, other
relevant City departments, and community partners to create a proposed protocol and
implementation plan to respond proactively with information and connections to resources
following instances of gun-related community trauma; and, be it
1O FURTHER RESOLVED, That the proposed protocol should include, at minimum, the
following:
1. Within 72 hours of the incident of gun violence, outreach through flyering, phone
calls, community events, or other means of reaching people within a one-block
radius from the incident to notify community members of available trauma
counseling resources;
2. A clear delineation of duties between departments, service providers, and any
other City-affiliated agencies as needed to implement the protocol; and, be it
FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors urges the proposed protocols
to be filed with the Board of Supervisors within 90 days of the passage of this Resolution and
be made publicly available for community input; and, be it
FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors urges a public hearing on the
resulting proposed protocol be held within 60 days of its filing with the Board.

WHEREAS, Pursuant to the Property and Business Improvement Law of 1994,
California Streets and Highways Code, Sections 36600, et seq. ("1994 Act"), as augmented
by Article 15A of the San Francisco Business and Tax Regulations Code ("Article 15A"), the
Board of Supervisors adopted () to approve a
management district plan ("the Management Plan") and engineer's report ("the Engineer's
Report") for the Dogpatch & Northwest Potrero Hill Green Benefit District ("the GBD"); and
WHEREAS, The Board of Supervisors adopted , which declared the
Board's intention to modify the Management Plan for the GBD, to allow for the allocation of
funds between Capital Improvement and Maintenance budget categories as described in the
proposed Amended Management Plan (dated ), and pursuant to a
Certification from the registered Engineer who prepared the original Engineer's Report, finding
that the proposed modification does not impose a new or increased assessment and does not
affect the conclusion in the Engineer's Report that the assessments are in proportion to the
special benefits received by each of the assessed parcels; the Resolution of Intention also
directed the Clerk of the Board of Supervisors to include copies of the Amended Management
Plan and Certification in , to set a public hearing on the proposed
modifications on , at 3:00 p.m., in the Board's Legislative Chamber located on
the Second Floor of City Hall, 1 Dr. Carlton B. Goodlett Place, San Francisco, California, and
to give notice of the public hearing as required by law; and
WHEREAS, The public hearing took place as noticed, the testimony of all interested
persons for or against was heard and considered, and a full, fair and complete meeting and
hearing was held; and
WHEREAS, The public interest, convenience, and necessity support the acceptance of
the proposed modifications to the Management Plan; now, therefore, be it
RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors declares as follows:
Section 1. Pursuant to Section 36636 of the 1994 Act, the Board of Supervisors
approves the Certification letter and approves the Amended Management Plan, so that the
Owners' Association can combine the Maintenance and Capital Improvement budget
categories and receive greater flexibility to allocate funds between those categories, as stated
in the Amended Management Plan. The proposed modifications do not alter the approved
boundary maps for the district, do not result in any new or increased assessments on any
parcels in the GBD, and do not materially change the special benefits that the GBD provides
to the assessed parcels. Reference may be made to the detailed maps and list of parcels
identified by Assessor Parcel Number that are contained in the Amended Management Plan,
in order to determine which specific parcels are in the GBD. A copy of the Amended
Management Plan and Certification letter are both on file with the Clerk of the Board of
Supervisors in , and are declared to be a part of this Resolution as if set forth
fully herein.
Section 2. Within the area encompassed by the GBD, the City currently provides
services at the same level provided to other similar areas of the City. It is the intent of the
Board of Supervisors to continue to provide the area encompassed by the GBD with the same
level of services provided to these other similar areas of the City. The proposed modification
of the Management Plan will not affect this policy.
Section 3. The Planning Department has determined that the actions contemplated in
this Resolution are in compliance with the California Environmental Quality Act (California
Public Resources Code, Sections 21000 et seq.). Said determination is on file with the Clerk
of the Board of Supervisors in and is declared to be a part of this Resolution
as if set forth fully herein.

Street, San Francisco, California, (the "Project"), to provide housing for persons and families
of low and very low income through the issuance of multifamily housing revenue bonds; and
WHEREAS, The City and County of San Francisco (the "City") is authorized to issue
revenue bonds for such purpose pursuant to the Charter of the City, Article I of Chapter 43 of
the Administrative Code of the City and, to the extent applicable, Chapter 7 of Part 5 of
Division 31 (commencing with Section 52075) of the Health and Safety Code of the State of
California ("Health and Safety Code"), as now in effect and as it may from time to time
hereafter be amended or supplemented (collectively, the "Act"); and
WHEREAS, Any Bonds (hereinafter defined) to be issued to finance the Project will be
limited obligations of the City, the sole source of repayment for which shall be payments made
by the Borrower or collateral security pledged by or for the Borrower, together with investment
income on certain funds and accounts; and
WHEREAS, The interest on the Tax-Exempt Bonds (hereinafter defined) may qualify
1O for tax exemption under Section 103 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended, (the
"Code"), only if the Tax-Exempt Bonds are approved in accordance with Section 147(f) of the
Code; and
WHEREAS, This Board is the elected legislative body of the City and is the applicable
elected representative required to approve the issuance of the Bonds within the meaning of
Section 147(f) of the Code; and
WHEREAS, On , the City published a notice on the City's website
regarding its intent to hold a public hearing with respect to the issuance of multifamily housing
revenue bonds in an amount not to exceed $90,000,000 to finance the Project, and said
hearing was held on , by the Mayor's Office of Housing and Community
Development and an opportunity was provided for persons to comment on the issuance of the
Bonds and the financing of the Project; and
WHEREAS, Thereafter, on , pursuant to , this
Board approved the issuance of multifamily housing revenue bonds, in an amount not to
exceed $90,000,000, for the purposes of Section 147(f) of the Code, declared its intent to
issue multifamily housing revenue bonds and authorized officers of the City to submit an
application and related documents to the California Debt Limit Allocation Committee
("CD LAC") and take other actions in connection with the proposed financing of the Project;
and
WHEREAS, On , CDLAC, in its , allocated
$71,076,486 in qualified private activity bond volume cap to the Project; and
WHEREAS, There has been prepared and presented to this Board for consideration at
this meeting the documentation required for the issuance of the Tax-Exempt Bonds (as
defined herein) and the Taxable Bonds (as defined herein, and together with the Tax-Exempt
Bonds, the "Bonds"), and such documentation is on file with the Clerk of the Board of
Supervisors (the "Clerk of the Board"); and
WHEREAS, It appears that each of the documents which is now before this Board is
substantially in appropriate form and is an appropriate instrument to be executed and
delivered for the purposes intended; and
WHEREAS, This Board finds that public interest and necessity require that the City at
this time make arrangements for the sale of the Bonds; and
WHEREAS, The City has engaged Squire Patton Boggs (US) LLP, and The Law Office
of Monica M. Baranovsky, as co-bond counsel with respect to the Bonds ("Co-Bond
Counsel"); and
WHEREAS, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. has expressed its intention to purchase, or
cause an affiliate to purchase, the Bonds authorized hereby; now, therefore, be it
RESOLVED, By this Board of Supervisors of the City and County of San Francisco as
follows:
Section 1. Approval of Recitals. This Board hereby finds and declares that the
recitals are true and correct.
Section 2. Approval of Issuance of Bonds. In accordance with the Act and the
Indenture (hereinafter defined), the City is hereby authorized to issue and deliver (i) tax-
exempt multifamily housing revenue bonds (the "Tax-Exempt Bonds") designated as "City and
County of San Francisco, California Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds (600-7th Street
Apartments) Series 2022B-1 ,"in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $71 ,076,486,
and (ii) taxable multifamily housing revenue bonds (the Taxable Bonds") designated as "City
and County of San Francisco, California Taxable Multifamily Housing Revenue Bonds (600-
7th Street Apartments) Series 2022B-2" in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed
$18,923,514; each with such additional or other designation as may be necessary or
1O appropriate to distinguish such series from every other series of bonds of the City, with an
interest rate not to exceed twelve percent (12%) per annum, and each with a final maturity
date not later than forty-five (45) years from the date of issuance of the Bonds. The Bonds
shall be in the form set forth in and otherwise in accordance with the Indenture, and shall be
executed by the manual signature of the Mayor of the City (the "Mayor") and as further
provided in the Indenture.
Section 3. Indenture. The Trust Indenture (the "Indenture"), by and between the City
and a trustee, to be determined after the adoption of this Resolution (the "Trustee"), in the
form presented to this Board, a copy of which is on file with the Clerk of the Board, is hereby
approved. Each of the Mayor, the Director of the Mayor's Office of Housing and Community
Development or any other Authorized City Representative (as such term is defined in the
Indenture) of the City (collectively, the "Authorized Officers") is hereby authorized to execute
the Indenture in said form, together with such additions thereto and changes therein as the
City Attorney and Co-Bond Counsel may approve or recommend in accordance with Section
hereof.
Section 4. Regulatory Agreement and Declaration of Restrictive Covenants. The
Regulatory Agreement and Declaration of Restrictive Covenants (the "Regulatory
Agreement"), by and between the City and the Borrower, in the form presented to this Board,
a copy of which is on file with the Clerk of the Board, is hereby approved. Each Authorized
Officer is hereby authorized to execute the Regulatory Agreement, in said form, together with
such additions thereto and changes therein as the City Attorney and Co-Bond Counsel may
Section 5. Approval of Loan Agreement. The Loan Agreement (the "Loan
Agreement"), by and between the City and the Borrower, in the form presented to this Board,
1O a copy of which is on file with the Clerk of the Board, is hereby approved. Each Authorized
Officer is hereby authorized to execute the Loan Agreement in said form, together with such
additions thereto and changes therein as the City Attorney and Co-Bond Counsel may
Section 6. Issuer Fees. The City, acting through the Mayor's Office of Housing and
Community Development, shall charge a fee for the administrative costs associated with
issuing the Bonds (the "Issuance Fee") in an amount not to exceed 0.25% of the maximum
aggregate principal amount of the Bonds. Such fee shall be payable at closing and may be
contingent on the issuance of the Bonds. The City shall also charge an annual fee (the
"Annual Fees") for monitoring compliance with the provisions of the Regulatory Agreement in
an amount not to exceed 0.125% of the outstanding aggregate principal amount of the Bonds,
but no less than $2,500 annually, for the term of the Regulatory Agreement. The Board
hereby authorizes the Mayor's Office of Housing and Community Development to charge and
collect, or appoint an agent, which may be the Trustee, to collect on behalf of the City, the
fees described in this section. Notwithstanding the foregoing provisions of this Section, the
City, acting through the Mayor's Office of Housing and Community Development, is
authorized to charge an Issuance Fee or Annual Fees, or both, that is or are lower than the
fees prescribed in this Section if, upon the advice of Co-Bond Counsel, lower fees are
necessary or advisable to ensure that the Tax-Exempt Bonds do not become "arbitrage
bonds" within the meaning of Section 148 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended,
or to ensure that interest on the Tax-Exempt Bonds does not become includable in gross
income for federal income tax purposes.
Section 7. Modifications, Changes, Additions. Any Authorized Officer executing the
Indenture, the Loan Agreement or the Regulatory Agreement (collectively, the "City
Agreements"), in consultation with the City Attorney and Co-Bond Counsel, is hereby
authorized to approve and make such modifications, changes or additions to the City
Agreements as may be necessary or advisable, provided that such modification does not
authorize an aggregate principal amount of the Tax-Exempt Bonds in excess of $71,076,486
and the Taxable Bonds in excess of $18,923,514, provide for a final maturity on either series
of Bonds later than forty-five (45) years from the date of issuance of the Bonds, or provide for
the Bonds to bear interest at a rate in excess of twelve percent (12%) per annum. The
approval of any modification, addition or change to any of the City Agreements shall be
evidenced conclusively by the execution and delivery of the document in question.
Section 8. Ratification. All actions heretofore taken by the officers and agents of the
City with respect to the sale, issuance and delivery of the Bonds, as consistent with the City
Agreements and this Resolution, are hereby approved, confirmed and ratified.
Section 9. General Authority. The proper officers of the City, including but not limited
to the Authorized Officers, are hereby authorized and directed, for and in the name and on
behalf of the City, to do any and all things and take any and all actions and execute and
deliver any and all certificates, agreements and other documents (including but not limited to
any certificates necessary to allocate a portion of the previously-obtained voter approval of
low rent housing projects pursuant to Article 34 of the State Constitution to the Project, if
applicable), subordinations, assignments, tax documents and those documents described in
the City Agreements, which they, or any of them, may deem necessary or advisable in order
to consummate the lawful issuance and delivery of the Bonds and to effectuate the purposes
thereof and of the City Agreements. Any such actions are solely intended to further the
purposes of this Resolution, and are subject in all respects to the terms of the Resolution. No
such actions shall increase the risk to the City or require the City to spend any resources not
otherwise granted herein. Final versions of any such documents shall be provided to the
Clerk of the Board for inclusion in the official file within 30 days of execution by all parties.
1O Section 10. File. All documents referenced herein as being on file with the Clerk of
the Board are located in , which is hereby declared to be a part of this
Resolution as set forth fully herein.

3 Resolution initiating a landmark designation under Article 10 of the Planning Code for

5 Cultural District.
6
7 WHEREAS, Under Planning Code, Section 100.4.1, the Board of Supervisors may by
8 resolution initiate landmark designation; and
9 WHEREAS, The intersection of Turk Street and Taylor Street (Turk & Taylor),
10 [LATITUDE: 37.78323 LONGITUDE: -122.41078], is situated in Supervisorial District 5 within
11 San Francisco's Transgender Cultural District in the Tenderloin neighborhood and is listed as
12 a historic site by the cultural district; and
13 WHEREAS, The Transgender District is the world's first legally-recognized cultural
14 district dedicated to the transgender, gender non-conforming, non-binary, and intersex
15 community and became a legally recognized cultural district in San Francisco in 2017; and
16 WHEREAS, The Turk & Taylor Streets Intersection witnessed the first documented
17 uprising of trans and queer people in August of 1966 known as the Compton's Cafeteria Riot
18 due to the fact that it started as a confrontation between a police officer and a drag queen at
19 Compton's Cafeteria at the intersection of Turk & Taylor and spilled out into the streets; and
20 WHEREAS, The corner of Turk & Taylor continues to be a valuable asset tethered to
21 the history of transgender and queer individuals in San Francisco's Tenderloin neighborhood
22 and is a key monument for The Transgender Cultural District; and
23 WHEREAS, The Turk & Taylor Streets Intersection is the site of the Black Trans Lives
24 Matter Mural, a visual demonstration calling for awareness of the alarming violence
25
Supervisors Preston; Mandelman, Melgar, Safai
BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Page 1
1 perpetrated against transgender women, and disproportionately impacting Black transgender
2 women; and
3 WHEREAS, San Francisco became the first city in the nation to recognize the month of
4 August as Transgender History Month in 2021 as part of an effort to formally recognize the
5 contributions of the transgender community including critical historical events, figures, and
6 places; and
7 WHEREAS, The Compton's Cafeteria Riots of 1966 transpired three years before the
8 Stonewall Inn Riots, which is regarded as the quintessential event for the gay liberation
9 movement, eclipsing other trailblazing events; and
10 WHEREAS, The revolutionary event that took place at the intersection of Turk & Taylor
11 Streets deserves recognition as a seminal event in the history of transgender liberation; and
12 WHEREAS, Even now, in 2022, the transgender community continues to face
13 persecution through unprecedented anti-trans legislation produced by conservative state
14 legislatures across the United States targeting transgender youth and access to gender
15 affirming medical services under the threat of legal persecution; and
16 WHEREAS, The Biden-Harris Administration advanced a resolution acknowledging
17 Transgender Day of Visibility (TDOV) and condemning the proliferation of detrimental anti
18 trans legislation, signaling a breakthrough in solidarity on behalf of the President of the United
19 States in regard to the continued marginalization and violence committed against the
20 transgender community; and
21 WHEREAS, Recognizing symbols and monuments tethered to transgender liberation
22 and activism support and empower an embattled community that struggles for equitable
23 representation in documented history; and
24 WHEREAS, The Turk & Taylor Streets Intersection represent a sacred site for the
25 transgender community capable of furthering social and historical awareness, educational

WHEREAS, Under the Stewart B. McKinney Homeless Assistance Act and Cranston
Gonzalez National Affordable Housing Act of 1990, the Secretary of the U.S. Department of
Housing and Urban Development (HUD) is authorized to make a grant to the City and County
of San Francisco under the Emergency Solutions Grants Program (ESG); and,
WHEREAS, The City and County of San Francisco anticipates receiving $1,587,675 in
FY2022-2023 ESG Program funds from HUD; and,
WHEREAS, The Citizen's Committee on Community Development (CCCD) has
prepared recommendations for ESG funding as set forth in a proposed Expenditure Schedule,
a copy of which is located in Clerk of the Board of Supervisors ; and,
WHEREAS, The ESG Program funds will be used to provide for the payment of certain
operating and social service expenses in connection with emergency shelters and for
homeless prevention activities; and,
WHEREAS, The proposed grant does not require an Annual Salary Ordinance
amendment; and,
WHEREAS, The funding agency (HUD) does not allow use of the grant on indirect
costs; now, therefore, be it
RESOLVED, That the Mayor of the City and County of San Francisco is hereby
authorized to apply for, accept, and expend the City's FY2022-2023 ESG Program entitlement
from HUD in accordance with the purposes and goals for the funding as generally set forth in
the 2020-24 Five-Year Consolidated Plan and the Expenditure Schedule; and, be it
FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors does hereby approve the
purposes and goals for FY2022-2023 ESG Program funding as set forth in the Expenditure
Schedule for recipient agencies and departments; and, be it
FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors hereby waives inclusion of
indirect costs in the grant budget; and, be it
FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Mayor is hereby authorized to enter into and execute
agreements between the City and County of San Francisco and various agencies consistent
with the ESG Program and the Expenditure Schedule; and, be it

and certifications as may be requested or required by HUD, and to take such additional
actions as may be required to apply for, accept and expend the ESG funds consistent with
this Resolution and the goals of the ESG Program and all applicable legal requirements, and
any such actions are solely intended to further the purposes of this Resolution, and are
subject in all respect to the terms of this Resolution, and any such action cannot increase the
risk to the City, or require the City to expend any resources, and that the Mayor shall consult
with the City Attorney prior to execution and provided that within 30 days of the agreements
approved by this Resolution being executed by all parties, such final documents (showing
marked changes, if any) shall be provided to the Clerk of the Board, for inclusion in the official
file, together with a brief explanation of any actions from the date of the adoption of this
Resolution; and, be it
FURTHER RESOLVED, That all actions heretofore taken by the officers of the City
with respect to the application for, or the acceptance or expenditure of, ESG funds, as

and ratified.

building located at 1170 Market Street, from , for a total term of , through , at a base rent of $75,000 per month, for a total
amount of $450,000 for six months; authorizing the Director of Property to execute
documents and take certain actions in furtherance of this Resolution; as defined
herein; and to authorize the Director of Property to enter into amendments or
modifications to the Lease that do not materially increase the obligations or liabilities
to the City and are necessary to effectuate the purposes of the Lease or this
Resolution.
WHEREAS, Deaths attributable to drug overdose in San Francisco have increased
over 200% since 2018; and
WHEREAS, A main contributor to the rapid rise in drug overdoses and deaths in San
Francisco is the recent increase in the prevalence of fentanyl in the illegal drug market which
is highly addictive and potent, and it is more likely to lead to overdose than other drugs; and
WHEREAS, On , Mayor London N. Breed issued a Proclamation
Declaring the Existence of a Local Emergency - Drug Overdoses in the Tenderloin which,
among other things, (1) allowed departments to procure services, goods, and public works
relating to the emergency using emergency procurement procedures, and waive any
applicable requirement of Civil Service Commission approval of such contracts, and
(2) allowed for the implementation in the Tenderloin of temporary facilities for purposes of
offering services as part of the emergency response ("Mayor's Declaration"); and
WHEREAS, On , the Board of Supervisors by Motion No. M21-183
concurred with the Mayor's Declaration of a Local Emergency; and
WHEREAS, Under the authority provided by the Mayor's Declaration, the Director of
Property, in consultation with the Director of the Department of Emergency Management
("DEM") and the City Attorney's Office, executed a six-month lease of the building located at
1170 Market Street (the "Premises"), for the period from , through , with 1170 Market Street, LLC, for City's use of the Premises as a Tenderloin Center in
the Tenderloin (the "Lease"); and
WHEREAS, A copy of the Lease is on file with the Clerk of the Board of Supervisors in
; and
WHEREAS, The Lease includes three extension options for the benefit of the City,
each for a term of two months, that are exercisable by the City subject to the approval of the
City's Board of Supervisors by Resolution; and
WHEREAS, The Tenderloin Center is a component of the Tenderloin Emergency
Initiative that aims to mitigate the widespread open-air drug use and lack of easily accessible
resources for people in the Tenderloin; and
WHEREAS, The Tenderloin Center is a services-focused location where people can
voluntarily go to find respite from the streets and gain access to a wide variety of resources
from the City and its partners; and
WHEREAS, The Tenderloin Center provides a safe, welcoming space for people who
suffer from substance use disorder in the Tenderloin to go where they can access dignity
services, social space, and help navigate City health and human services resources to link to
those services easily and quickly; and
WHEREAS, The Tenderloin Center was originally managed under the direction of
DEM, but DEM will now transfer management to the Department of Public Health ("DPH");
and
WHEREAS, DPH has determined that the Premises continue to be an ideal space and
location for the Tenderloin Center in furtherance of the City's Tenderloin Emergency
Intervention Plan; and
WHEREAS, DPH desires to continue the operations at the Tenderloin Center through
December31,2022;and
WHEREAS, Under the Lease, base rent payable by City will remain at $75,000 per
month ($2.022 per square foot) during this extension period; and
WHEREAS, The Director of Property has determined that an appraisal is not required
under Administrative Code, Section 23.27, because the Director of Property has determined
that the base rent will be at or below the fair market rental value of the Premises, and is below
$45 per square foot; and
WHEREAS, Funding in Fiscal Year 2022-2023 is subject to the enactment of the
annual appropriation Ordinance; and
WHEREAS, The Planning Department has determined that the Premises' temporary
use as The Tenderloin Linkage Center is consistent with the Eight Priority Policies of Planning
Code Section 101.1 and is, on balance, in conformity with the Objectives and Policies of the
General Plan; and
WHEREAS, The City, at its cost, will be responsible for maintenance of the interior of
the Premises, and for certain utilities and services, as set forth in the Lease; now, therefore,
RESOLVED, That in accordance with the recommendation of the Director of Health
and the Director of Property, the Board of Supervisors approves the exercise of all three
Lease extension options, and authorizes the Director of Property to take all actions necessary
to extend the Lease and to take such additional actions that are necessary or advisable to
effectuate the purpose of this Resolution; and, be it
FURTHER RESOLVED, That as set forth in the Lease, City will indemnify, defend, and
hold harmless Landlord from and against any and all claims, losses, and damages resulting
from the City's use of the Premises, any default by City of its obligations under the Lease, and
any negligent acts or omissions of City, its agents or invitees in or about the Premises; and,
FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors affirms and adopts as its own,
1O the findings made by the Planning Department in the General Plan Determination, on file with
the Clerk of the Board of Supervisors in and is incorporated herein by
reference; and, be it
FURTHER RESOLVED, That all actions previously taken by the officers of the City with
respect to the Lease are hereby approved, confirmed, and ratified; and, be it
FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors authorizes the Director of
Property to enter into any extensions, amendments, or modifications to the Lease (including
without limitation, the exhibits) that the Director of Property determines, in consultation with
the Director of Health and the City Attorney's Office, are in the best interest of the City, do not
materially increase the obligations or liabilities of the City, are necessary or advisable to
effectuate the purposes of the Lease or this Resolution, and are in compliance with all
applicable laws, including City's Charter.

3 Resolution renaming Hahn Street, between Visitacion Avenue and Sunnydale Avenue,
4 to "Mrs. Jackson Way;" with additional post passage directives to Public Works,
5 Municipal Transportation Agency, and the County Surveyor.
6
7 WHEREAS, Dr. Ruth Marie Jackson was a loving mother, grandmother, sister, aunt,
8 cousin, friend, and community leader in Sunnydale and the larger Visitacion Valley
9 neighborhood for more than five decades; and
10 WHEREAS, Dr. Ruth Marie Jackson owned and operated a licensed home daycare
11 offering childcare and play experiences for more than four decades; and
12 WHEREAS, Dr. Ruth Marie Jackson was an education specialist with the San
13 Francisco Unified School District for over 22 years serving the people of San Francisco; and
14 WHEREAS, The annual, daylong celebration began in 1998 when then Mayor Willie
15 Brown dedicated Ruth Jackson Family Day in honor of the longtime educator and Visitacion
16 Valley community leader; and
17 WHEREAS, Dr. Ruth Marie Jackson received her Honorary Doctorate in Humanities
18 from Sacramento Theological Seminary & Bible College on June 29, 2019; and
19 WHEREAS, Dr. Ruth Marie Jackson established the parade and fair, to bring local
20 families together and break the invisible barriers dividing the community; and
21 WHEREAS, Visitacion Valley, located in the far southeastern portion of San Francisco,
22 is both isolated and racked by poverty; and
23 WHEREAS, The Sunnydale neighborhood, which was originally built as temporary
24 housing for returning soldiers after World War II, is the largest public housing project in the
I
25 I! city; and
Supervisors Walton; Chan, Safai

2 for her lifelong commitment to public service; and

4 the age of 77; and

FILE NO. 220397 RESOLUTION NO. 263-22
1 [Supporting California State Senate Bill Nos. 929, 965, 970, 1035, 1154, 1227, 1238, and
1416 (Eggman) - Legislation Modernizing California's Behavioral Health Continuum]
2
3 Resolution urging the California State Legislature to pass California State Senate Bill
4 Nos. 929,965,970, 1035, 1154, 1227, 1238, and 1416, introduced by California Senator
5 Susan Eggman, on legislation modernizing California's Behavioral Health Continuum.
6
7 WHEREAS, California State Senate Bill Nos. (SB) 929, SB 965, SB 970, SB 1034, SB
8 1154, SB 1227, SB 1238, and SB 1416 constitute a package of bills introduced by Senator
9 Susan Eggman to improve California's behavioral health system across the continuum,
10 through prevention and early intervention, community supports and services, intersystem
11 collaboration, improving access to assisted outpatient treatment, providing increased
12 accountability through outcome tracking, preventing avoidable conservatorships, and
13 improving the effectiveness of our conservatorship process for those that need them; and
14 WHEREAS, Passage of these bills would represent a significant overhaul of
15 California's response to the behavioral health needs of individuals suffering from severe
16 mental illness; and
17 WHEREAS, The changes incorporated into Senator Eggman's legislation are
18 necessary and overdue; and
19 WHEREAS, The effects of California's failure to provide adequate mental health care is
20 reflected in the fact that 81 % of the unhoused, unsheltered people living on San Francisco's
21 streets suffer from some sort of psychiatric condition, addiction, or both, and our local
22 psychiatric emergency services have been on condition-red since May 2020; and
23 WHEREAS, SB 929 would require the State to collect data on the number of people
24 placed on temporary psychiatric holds, clinic outcomes for individuals placed in each type of
25 hold, and services provided in each category; and
Supervisors Mandelman; Safai
BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Page 1
1 WHEREAS, SB 965 would ensure that the court considers the contents of reports filed
2 at the conclusion of conservatorship investigations and that, during conservatorship
3 proceedings, relevant testimony may be considered, provided it falls under a hearsay
4 exemption; and
5 WHEREAS, SB 970 would amend the Mental Health Services Act to establish a clear
6 guide of measurable outcomes that counties can use to identify goals and create mechanisms
7 for counties to track and report on their performance, followed by promulgation of self
8 improvement plans and regular progress updates; and
9 WHEREAS, SB 1035 would explicitly allow courts to order medication as part of a
10 treatment plan, an essential tool that allows individuals to safely remain in their communities
11 and manage their mental illness; and
12 WHEREAS, SB 1154 would establish a real-time online dashboard to collect,
13 aggregate, and display information about beds in inpatient psychiatric facilities, crisis
14 stabilization units, residential community mental health facilities, and licensed residential
15 community mental health facilities; and
16 WHEREAS, SB 1227 would provide additional flexibility for counties in treating
17 individuals placed on 14-day psychiatric holds by allowing a second 30-day extension for
18 patients who do not stabilize after an additional 14-day hold and 30-day extension; and
19 WHEREAS, SB 1238 would require the Department of Health Care Services to
20 determine existing and projected needs for behavioral health services on a regional basis, and
21 would require councils of local governments to provide data on total bed capacity, total
22 utilization, and unmet need in a variety of categories; and
23 WHEREAS, SB 1416 would modernize the Lanterman-Petris-Short Act by defining
24 those who, as a result of a mental health disorder, are unable to provide for their basic needs

Resolution urging the California State Legislature to pass California State Senate Bill
Nos. 929,965,970, 1035, 1154, 1227, 1238, and 1416, introduced by California Senator
Susan Eggman, on legislation modernizing California's Behavioral Health Continuum.
WHEREAS, California State Senate Bill Nos. (SB) 929, SB 965, SB 970, SB 1034, SB
1154, SB 1227, SB 1238, and SB 1416 constitute a package of bills introduced by Senator
Susan Eggman to improve California's behavioral health system across the continuum,
through prevention and early intervention, community supports and services, intersystem
collaboration, improving access to assisted outpatient treatment, providing increased
accountability through outcome tracking, preventing avoidable conservatorships, and
improving the effectiveness of our conservatorship process for those that need them; and
WHEREAS, Passage of these bills would represent a significant overhaul of
California's response to the behavioral health needs of individuals suffering from severe
mental illness; and
WHEREAS, The changes incorporated into Senator Eggman's legislation are
necessary and overdue; and
WHEREAS, The effects of California's failure to provide adequate mental health care is
reflected in the fact that 81 % of the unhoused, unsheltered people living on San Francisco's
streets suffer from some sort of psychiatric condition, addiction, or both, and our local
psychiatric emergency services have been on condition-red since May 2020; and
WHEREAS, SB 929 would require the State to collect data on the number of people
placed on temporary psychiatric holds, clinic outcomes for individuals placed in each type of
hold, and services provided in each category; and
WHEREAS, SB 965 would ensure that the court considers the contents of reports filed
at the conclusion of conservatorship investigations and that, during conservatorship
proceedings, relevant testimony may be considered, provided it falls under a hearsay
exemption; and
WHEREAS, SB 970 would amend the Mental Health Services Act to establish a clear
guide of measurable outcomes that counties can use to identify goals and create mechanisms
for counties to track and report on their performance, followed by promulgation of self
improvement plans and regular progress updates; and
WHEREAS, SB 1035 would explicitly allow courts to order medication as part of a
treatment plan, an essential tool that allows individuals to safely remain in their communities
and manage their mental illness; and
WHEREAS, SB 1154 would establish a real-time online dashboard to collect,
aggregate, and display information about beds in inpatient psychiatric facilities, crisis
stabilization units, residential community mental health facilities, and licensed residential
community mental health facilities; and
WHEREAS, SB 1227 would provide additional flexibility for counties in treating
individuals placed on 14-day psychiatric holds by allowing a second 30-day extension for
patients who do not stabilize after an additional 14-day hold and 30-day extension; and
WHEREAS, SB 1238 would require the Department of Health Care Services to
determine existing and projected needs for behavioral health services on a regional basis, and
would require councils of local governments to provide data on total bed capacity, total
utilization, and unmet need in a variety of categories; and
WHEREAS, SB 1416 would modernize the Lanterman-Petris-Short Act by defining
those who, as a result of a mental health disorder, are unable to provide for their basic needs
of personal or medical care or self protection and safety, as "gravely disabled;" and
WHEREAS, This package of legislation is endorsed by the Big City Mayors coalition,
representing the 13 largest cities and roughly 11 million residents in California; now, therefore,
be it
RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors supports California Senate Bill Nos. 929,
965,970, 1035, 1154, 1227, 1238, and 1416; and, be it
FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors hereby directs the Clerk of the
Board to transmit a copy of this Resolution to San Francisco's state legislative delegation, and
the Office of the Chief Clerk of the Assembly and Office of the Secretary of the Senate.

title: Resolution changing the street name of Sonora Lane, between O’Farrell Street and Terra Anza Avenue, in the Anza Vista neighborhood, to “Vicha Ratanapakdee Way.”
raw_text:
FILE NO. 220248 RESOLUTION NO. 235-22
1 [Street Name Change - Sonora Lane to Vicha Ratanapakdee Way]
2
3 Resolution changing the street name of Sonora Lane, between O'Farrell Street and
4 Terra Anza Avenue, in the Anza Vista neighborhood, to "Vicha Ratanapakdee Way."
5
6 WHEREAS, On October 19, 2021, the Board of Supervisors adopted Resolution No.
7 489-21, declaring the Board's intent to rename Sonora Lane, between O'Farrell Street and
8 Terra Anza Avenue, to "Vicha Ratanapakdee Way," and directing the Department of Public
9 Works to initiate the City's street naming procedures; and
1O WHEREAS, Sonora Lane is the existing name of the public right-of-way between
11 O'Farrell Street and Terra Anza Avenue, and runs parallel to Anza Vista and St. Joseph's
12 Avenues, and is perpendicular to O'Farrell Street and Terra Anza Avenue; and
13 WHEREAS, Sonora Lane is in the Anza Vista neighborhood and near what was the
14 home of Mr. Vicha Ratanapakdee, and which remains the home of his family; and
15 WHEREAS, Mr. Ratanapakdee was an 84-year-old immigrant from Thailand who was
16 well known in the Anza Vista neighborhood for his hour-long walks each morning, a ritual that
17 kept him vibrant and healthy during the COVID-19 pandemic; and
18 WHEREAS, On January 28, 2021, Mr. Ratanapakdee, while walking peacefully in the
19 neighborhood, was suddenly and violently shoved to the pavement by an assailant, resulting
20 in severe head injuries from which Mr. Ratanapakdee tragically died shortly after the attack;
21 and
22 WHEREAS, Stop AAPI Hate, a California-based coalition, has recorded nearly 7,000
23 hate incidents involving Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders nationwide since the beginning
24 of the COVID-19 pandemic; and
25
Supervisors Stefani; Mandelman, Mar, Dorsey
BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Page 1
1 WHEREAS, Since Mr. Ratanapakdee's passing, his daughter has dedicated herself to
2 working to ensure survivors of these attacks and their families are supported through city
3 services, law enforcement, and the justice system; and
4 WHEREAS, Mr. Ratanapakdee's daughter has also worked to amplify the voices of
5 Asian Americans and the Thai and Southeast Asian communities through her participation in
6 marches, rallies, and many #stopAAPIHate events; and
7 WHEREAS, Renaming Sonora Lane to "Vicha Ratanapakdee Lane" would
8 commemorate and memorialize Mr. Ratanapakdee's death as a symbol of a movement
9 towards equality, anti-discrimination, and solidarity with the Asian American and Pacific
1O Islander Community, and as a reminder of the importance of peace among all peoples, in
11 accordance with Mr. Ratanapakdee's deepest values; and
12 WHEREAS, The Department of Public Works conducted a review and investigation of
13 the proposed street name change as directed under Resolution No. 489-21, finding that the
14 proposed street name does not exist in the City's current list of official street names, and
15 therefore does not warrant objection under Public Works Code, Section 423, and further
16 finding that, pursuant to the process for changing street names set forth in the "Establishing
17 Street Names" bulletin posted on the Department's webpage, no City Agencies or fronting
18 property owners object to the proposed name change; and
19 WHEREAS, On January 20, 2022, the Department of Public Works notified the Clerk of
20 the Board of Supervisors that it had completed its investigation into the proposed renaming of
21 Sonora Lane, the only segment of which runs between Terra Vista Avenue and O'Farrell
22 Street, and the results of which investigation are on file with the Clerk of the Board in File No.
23 210885, the file for this Resolution; and
24 WHEREAS, In compliance with the requirement of California Streets and Highways
25 Code, Section 970.5, notice of a public hearing was posted at least 10 days prior to the
Supervisors Stefani; Mandelman, Mar, Dorsey
BOARD OF SUPERVISORS Page
1 hearing on this Resolution before the Land Use and Transportation Committee, in at least
2 three public places along the street proposed to be affected by the renaming; now, therefore,
3 be it
4 RESOLVED, That pursuant to its authority under California Government Code, Section
5 34091.1 and California Streets and Highways Code, Sections 970.5 and 5026, the Board of
6 Supervisors hereby renames Sonora Lane, between Terra Vista Avenue and O'Farrell Street,
7 to "Vicha Ratanapakdee Way" to honor Mr. Ratanapakdee's legacy, and to make clear that
8 the City and County of San Francisco stands with its Asian American Pacific Islander
9 communities during this extraordinarily difficult time for those communities; and, be it
10 FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors directs the Municipal
11 Transportation Agency to erect street signs in accordance with Transportation Code, Section
12 2.2, which signs should indicate both the new and the former names of the street affected by
13 this Resolution-the new street name, "Vicha Ratanapakdee Way," in large letters and the
14 former name, "Sonora Lane," in smaller letters above or beneath the new name-and such
15 signs indicating the two street names shall remain posted for five years and then replaced
16 with signs indicating only the new street name "Vicha Ratanapakdee Way;" and, be it
17 FURTHER RESOLVED, That in adopting this legislation, the Board of Supervisors
18 does not intend to effectuate any change in City department jurisdictional control over the
19 public right-of-way to be renamed as "Vicha Ratanapakdee Way;" and, be it
20 FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors directs the Clerk of the Board
21 to promptly forward a copy of this Resolution to the County Surveyor in accordance with
22 California Streets and Highways Code, Section 5026, and that the County Surveyor include
23 the new street name on the Official Map of the City; and, be it
24 FURTHER RESOLVED, That the Board of Supervisors directs the Department of
25 Public Works to add "Vicha Ratanapakdee Way" to the City's official list of street names.

title: Resolution authorizing the Recreation and Park Department to accept and expend cash and/or in-kind grants from the San Francisco Parks Alliance (SFPA) valued at up to $400,000 for restoration projects in the Japanese Tea Garden project for the project term of upon approval of Board of Supervisors until Notice of Substantial Completion.

Restoration Projects - Valued Up to $400,000]

3 Resolution authorizing the Recreation and Park Department to accept and expend cash
4 and/or in-kind grants from the San Francisco Parks Alliance (SFPA) valued at up
5 to $400,000 for restoration projects in the Japanese Tea Garden project for the project
6 term of upon approval of Board of Supervisors until Notice of Substantial Completion.

8 WHEREAS, The City, through the Recreation and Park Department (RPO), operates
9 and maintains The Japanese Tea Garden in Golden Gate Park (Garden), located in
10 Supervisorial District 1; and
11 WHEREAS, The Friends of the Japanese Tea Garden, in partnership with the RPO,
12 launched the Japanese Tea Garden Revitalization Campaign; the Friends of the Japanese
13 Tea Garden is a fiscally sponsored group of the San Francisco Parks Alliance (SFPA); the
14 Revitalization Campaign will focus on the restoration of the Pagoda, as well as other priority
15 projects which improve access to and enhance the Pagoda, including the landscaped area
16 around the Pagoda, the Long Bridge, and the Temple Gate; and
17 WHEREAS, The estimated cost for the restoration projects in the Garden is
18 approximately $2,000,000; the Department has budgeted a total of $1,700,000 for the
19 projects; the SFPA, on behalf of the Friends of the Japanese Tea Garden, has offered to raise
20 the remaining funds, estimated to be approximately $300,000; if there are additional costs and
21 if there are additional philanthropic funds, the Friends group has offered to donate up
22 to $400,000 (Grant); and
23 WHEREAS, On July 15, 2021, the Recreation and Park Commission, by Resolution

25 expend the cash and/or in-kind grants; now, therefore, be it
